item.title: Brazil stocks, real tumble as Lula win shifts investor focus
item.description: Brazil's real tumbled over 11% against the US dollar in early spot trading, one of its biggest daily declines on record.
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Campos, Marcela Ayres, Karin Strohecker
item.content:encoded: Brazilian stocks and the real currency posted historic losses on Monday after the surprise [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"reelection"] of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva reversed recent market bets on a right-wing ascent to power. Brazil's real tumbled over 11% against the US dollar in early spot trading, one of its biggest daily declines on record, while the benchmark Bovespa stock index (.BVSP) was down more than 15% in its largest daily percentage drop since 1998. The selloff also hit [USN:L5N46C0GQ TEXT:"sovereign debt"], with longer-dated bonds hit hardest and the 2054 maturity down 2.5 cents to yield 7.45% as Brazil's fiscal path came into focus. "Lula’s victory triggered a sharp market selloff as investors reassessed the fiscal outlook under his fourth term,” Mauricio Monge, senior Latin America economist at Oxford Economics, said in a report. His biggest challenge, Monge wrote, "will be to convince markets that he can deliver a credible, sustainable fiscal adjustment while prioritizing real wage growth and employment." VIOLENT VOLATILITY Trading on Brazil's stock exchange was halted for 30 minutes after the Bovespa index fell 10% from its last close, triggering the market's circuit breaker mechanism, stock exchange operator B3 said in a statement. The move came after B3 initially expanded the daily trading limits for Bovespa stock index futures, dollar futures and interest rate futures in response to heightened market volatility. Brazil's five-year credit default swaps, a measure of the cost of insuring against sovereign default, [USN:L5N46C14U TEXT:"jumped to 151.67 basis points"] from Friday's close of 120.21, S&P Global Market Intelligence data showed. As markets tumbled, the Brazilian Treasury cancelled its regular auctions of inflation-linked and fixed-rate government bonds scheduled for October 27 and October 29, respectively. The local real was down 8.3% to the dollar at 5.4274 per greenback. Prices of raw sugar, of which Brazil is a major exporter, slid 5.6% on the collapsing exchange rate. The plunge is a sharp reversal from the rally seen earlier this month, when markets soared on expectations of a shift to the right after Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, unexpectedly finished first in the opening round of Brazil's presidential elections. The Bovespa closed on Friday almost 7% above its level before the first-round vote, while the real currency had been nearly 5% stronger against the US dollar over that period. Interest rate futures had also reflected expectations that tighter fiscal policy in the event of a Bolsonaro government would make room for lower borrowing costs. Senator Bolsonaro's refusal to concede and his pledge to seek an annulment added to investor uncertainty. "Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result, or at least allows the constitution to run its course," said Chris Turner, strategist at ING in London. CHALLENGES AHEAD Attention will now turn to Lula's choice of finance minister and what it signals about his fiscal approach. "The key signal for markets will be the next Lula administration's commitment to fiscal discipline, starting with the appointment of a new finance minister in coming weeks," said Graham Stock at RBC BlueBay Asset Management. Lula faces the [USN:L1N468127 TEXT:"challenge"] of slowing the rise in Brazil's debt while protecting social programmes and investment, with investors looking for signs his gradual fiscal approach can bring borrowing costs down. "(The) Lula administration will have no choice but to do some fiscal consolidation too, but most investors doubt it will be enough to put debt sustainability back on track," said Thierry Larose, portfolio manager at Vontobel. Without confidence that Lula can deliver, lenders could demand higher interest rates, adding to Brazil's debt burden and making credit more expensive for businesses and households. "Investors want a clear and credible commitment to fiscal discipline," said Alejo Czerwonko, chief investment officer for emerging markets at UBS Global Wealth Management. "We expect the rally that followed the first round to be largely priced out, and sentiment to stay weak until a clear fiscal plan emerges," Czerwonko said, adding that investors wanted a believable path to stabilize public debt. The reelected president's team has said it aims to produce a budget surplus of about 1.3% of gross domestic product by 2030. "Lula's policies have talked about spending cuts," said Divya Singaravelu, head of research at Meridian 1305 Capital, "but he has not gone into the details of how that is going to look."

item.title: ＳＫハイニックス、28日に株主還元策発表へ 特別配当報道受け
item.description: [ソウル ２６日 ロイター] - 韓国半導体大手ＳＫハイニックスは、四半期決算を公表する２８日に株主還元策を発表すると...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ＳＫハイニックス、28日に株主還元策発表へ　特別配当報道受け 10/26 12:46 配信

韓国・ソウルで開催された半導体展示会に設置されたSKハイニックスのブース。2026年10月16日撮影　REUTERS/Kim Hong-Ji

[ソウル ２６日 ロイター] - 韓国半導体大手ＳＫハイニックスは、四半期決算を公表する２８日に株主還元策を発表すると明らかにした。約１６兆ウォン（１２０億ドル）の特別配当を検討しているとの報道を受けた。

韓国紙の東亜日報は２６日、ＳＫハイニックスが日本の半導体メモリーメーカー、キオクシアホールディングスの株式売却益を原資に特別配当を検討していると報じた。

ＳＫハイニックスは今年完了した株式売却の詳細を公表していないが、アナリストは、累計で多額の投資利益を計上したと推定している。

同社は２０１８年、米投資会社ベインキャピタルが主導する日米韓の投資家連合を通じ、キオクシアに約４兆ウォンを投資した。

ＳＫハイニックスは報道について証券取引所から問われた際、「さまざまな株主還元策を検討している」とし、２８日に第３・四半期決算と合わせて発表する予定だと説明した。詳細には踏み込まなかった。

米エヌビディアに製品を供給するＳＫハイニックスとサムスン電子は、人工知能（ＡＩ）向けメモリー半導体の需要急増を背景に過去最高益を計上し、配当や自社株買いを通じて余剰資金をより多く還元するよう投資家からの圧力が強まっている。

ＳＫハイニックスは８月、４０兆ウォン相当の自社株買いおよび消却を実施し、２５─２７年に生み出されるフリーキャッシュフローの５０％超を株主還元の拡充に充てると発表した。

また同社は２３日、市場の変動を理由に、半導体子会社ソリダイムの米国上場計画を一時停止したと発表した。この計画には投資家や規制当局から懸念が示され、同社株の重荷となっていた。

item.title: EXCLUSIVE-ＳＨＥＩＮ、米ＦＴＣと1億ドルで和解へ 顧客の苦情巡る調査で
item.description:
Helen Reid Jody Godoy
[ロンドン ２３日 ロイター] - 中国発のファストファッションネット通販...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE-ＳＨＥＩＮ、米ＦＴＣと1億ドルで和解へ　顧客の苦情巡る調査で 10/26 12:31 配信

Sheinのロゴ。英リバプールで2024年12月14日撮影　 REUTERS/Phil Noble

Helen Reid　Jody Godoy

[ロンドン ２３日 ロイター] - 中国発のファストファッションネット通販大手ＳＨＥＩＮ（シーイン）は、配送の遅延など顧客の苦情に関する米連邦取引委員会（ＦＴＣ）の調査について、１億ドルを支払って和解することに同意した。関係筋が２３日、ロイターに明らかにした。

和解金は同社の第２・四半期利益の４４％に相当。欧米で規制や税制面の締め付けに直面し、成長に急ブレーキがかかる同社にとって新たな打撃となる。

シーインはロイターに対する声明で「ＦＴＣと建設的な結論に達した」と述べ、近く追加情報を公表すると表明した。ＦＴＣの報道官はコメントを控えた。

同社は７月、香港上場に向けた提出書類で、米国の調査により多額の罰金を科される可能性があると警告していた。

ロイターが確認したＦＴＣの記録によると、２０２０年１月から２６年６月にかけて、総額１１００万ドル超の購入に関し、消費者から１万２０００件余りの苦情が寄せられていた。

苦情の一部は、配達済みと表示された荷物が顧客に届かず、シーインのカスタマーサービスも問題を解決しなかったなど、配送に関する内容だった。

ロイターは苦情の内容や、それらが最終的に解決されたかを独自に検証することはできなかった。

シーインは欧州連合（ＥＵ）で少額小包に３ユーロの手数料を課されたことなどで業績が打撃を受け、株価は９月１日の香港上場以来２２％下落している。ＥＵは１１月１日から２ユーロの追加取扱手数料を課す予定だ。

item.title: Saudi defence pact countries push for peace in Tehran as Houthis launch more attacks
item.description: Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis launched new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved defence support for the Gulf kingdom.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Mills, Ariba Shahid, Menna Alaaeldin
item.content:encoded: Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis [USN:L2N46C045 TEXT:"launched new attacks"] on Saudi Arabia and Egypt [USN:S8N44701K TEXT:"approved defence support"] for the Gulf kingdom. The talks were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations — which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August — since a war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran also spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen. Saudi Arabia said the visit was intended to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation". It was represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said. Iranian state media published pictures of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, attending the meetings. At the conclusion, the four states agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation in peace and security, state media reported. Pakistan and Qatar have led mediation efforts in the war. Earlier efforts helped produce an [USN:L6N42N0OL TEXT:"interim peace agreement"] in June, but fighting between Iran and the US soon resumed. Conflict then flared between the Iran-aligned Houthis and US ally Saudi Arabia, opening a new front. US AND IRAN THREATEN NEW ATTACKS The wider fighting has restricted shipping through the energy chokepoint of the [USN:L8N3YO10W TEXT:"Strait of Hormuz"], pushed up [USN:L2N46B09G TEXT:"global oil and gas prices"], left Gulf states facing missile and drone attacks, and caused a new [USN:L6N46C0OE TEXT:"humanitarian crisis"] in Yemen. Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened recently, with President Donald Trump [USN:L1N469125 TEXT:"saying on Friday"] the US may strike Iran again. Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had [USN:L6N46816Q TEXT:"drawn up detailed plans"] to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel attack again. The war, which earlier in the year also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese Hezbollah militia, has eroded Trump's approval ratings ahead of the US [USN:L6N46017L TEXT:"midterm elections"] that decide control of Congress. Iranian security chief Rezaei said the visit by the three countries had shown that "American threats have little impact on countries around the world". He spoke of a "new and positive atmosphere" in the region. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei had earlier said the meeting, proposed when Munir visited Tehran [USN:L1N4660R4 TEXT:"last week"], could be a first step towards establishing regional security mechanisms. A senior Pakistani security official said the focus was on building a regional non-aggression network. The agenda also included US-Iran talks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports, they said. Another Pakistani official said Munir, with a go-ahead from Trump to try diplomacy, had presented Iran with a solution to the conflict that would offer something to both the US and Iran, without giving details. The Mecca pact states and Qatar could act as guarantors if it was accepted, the official added. An Iranian official had earlier said there would be [USN:S8N42207J TEXT:"no discussion"] of Iran's [USN:L1N45T0JD TEXT:"nuclear programme"] at Monday's meeting, and the issue would not be addressed until Tehran's demands for ending the war were met. Those conditions include ending a US blockade of Iranian ports and lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports. US Vice President JD Vance [USN:L1N45T0DK TEXT:"has said"] Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war. Pakistan's military media office and Turkey's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. PARLIAMENT APPROVES EGYPTIAN DEFENCE SUPPORT FOR SAUDIS Saudi Arabia has intensified strikes against the Houthis since they captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing against Saudi-backed government forces. The Houthis have hit Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities. On Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as well as Riyadh airport, which said it had [USN:L2N46A05D TEXT:"resumed operations"] at two terminals a day earlier. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks. Parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the Mecca pact, on Monday authorised the Egyptian military to help defend Saudi Arabia, a major financial and political partner for Cairo. The [USN:L6N4440IT TEXT:"Mecca Joint Defence Agreement"] says signatories shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters. The pact's members held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and [USN:L1N45R0S7 TEXT:"agreed to ensure"] the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

item.title: Australia's Perfection Fresh to seek $8.4 million penalty over price fixing, regulator says
item.description: Perfection Fresh Pty, Australia's second-largest vegetable supplier, admitted to fixing prices of vegetables sold to ALDI and agreed with the competition regulator to jointly seek a A$12 million ($8.43 million) penalty in court, the regulator said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Perfection Fresh Pty, Australia's second-largest vegetable supplier, admitted to fixing prices of vegetables sold to ALDI and agreed with the competition regulator to jointly seek a A$12 million ($8.43 million) penalty in court, the regulator said on Monday. Here are some details: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said Perfection Fresh admitted to fixing prices of broccoli, cauliflower and iceberg lettuce supplied to ALDI in New South Wales on 11 occasions between 2019 and 2020 The proposed A$12 million penalty covers nine contraventions and one attempted contravention of Australia's competition laws, the ACCC added The Federal Court will decide at a later date whether the proposed penalty and other orders are appropriate, the regulator said in its statement Perfection Fresh said in an emailed response it has reached an agreement with the ACCC concerning price fixing and has taken steps to strengthen its leadership, governance and compliance systems The ACCC began proceedings in September 2025 against Perfection Fresh, three other suppliers and three individuals over alleged price fixing. The case against the other parties is ongoing. ($1 = 1.4241 Australian dollars)

item.title: 中国百度と米リフト、27年ロンドンでロボタクシー商用化目指す
item.description:
Marissa Davison
[ロンドン ２３日 ロイター] - 米配車大手リフト傘下のフリーナウと中国ＩＴ大手・百...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
中国百度と米リフト、27年ロンドンでロボタクシー商用化目指す 10/26 11:54 配信

写真は百度の「アポロＲＴ６」。2022年7月、中国・北京で撮影。 REUTERS/Yingzhi Yang

Marissa Davison

[ロンドン ２３日 ロイター] - 米配車大手リフト傘下のフリーナウと中国ＩＴ大手・百度（バイドゥ）傘下のアポロ・ゴーは２２日、ロンドンでバイドゥの自動運転車「ＲＴ６」を公開し、２０２７年に同市で自動運転タクシー（ロボタクシー）事業の開始を目指すと発表した。

フリーナウとアポロ・ゴーは、この夏ロンドンで安全運転手を同乗させた車両の試験走行を開始しており、来年には完全無人走行車両を市内で走らせたいとしている。

米上院が米国内での中国製自動車の販売を恒久的に禁止する法案の可決に向けて動く中、リフトとバイドゥはロンドンでの提携を発表した。米国のこうした動きを背景に、欧州に注力する企業は増えている。

ロンドンではロボタクシー商用化を巡る競争が激化しており、英国の自動運転スタートアップのウェイブと米配車大手ウーバー・テクノロジーズは９月に、ロンドンでロボタクシー事業を、当初は安全運転手を乗せた状態で開始。米グーグルの親会社アルファベット傘下のロボタクシー企業、ウェイモも年内にロンドンにおける完全無人車両による配車サービスの開始を目標としている。

フリーナウの英事業責任者ダニー・オゴーマン氏は、ロンドンはスピードバンプが多く、道幅が狭いほか、制限速度が時速２０マイル（約３２キロ）の道路が多いため、試験には特に適していると指摘。「車両は、まるで自分が運転免許試験に合格しようとする時と同じように交通ルールを学ぶ段階にある」と説明した。

オゴーマン氏によると、フリーナウはロンドン交通局と緊密に連携しており、２６日の週にも規制ガイドラインが示される見込み。

item.title: 午前の日経平均は続落、複数イベント控え方向感欠く ＴＯＰＩＸはプラス
item.description:
Noriyuki Hirata
[東京 ２６日 ロイター] - 前場の東京株式市場で日経平均は続落し、前営業日比０．７...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
午前の日経平均は続落、複数イベント控え方向感欠く　ＴＯＰＩＸはプラス 10/26 11:50 配信

写真は2024年12月、都内の東京証券取引所で撮影。 REUTERS/Kim Kyung-Hoon

Noriyuki Hirata

[東京 ２６日 ロイター] - 前場の東京株式市場で日経平均は続落し、前営業日比０．７６％（４７８円５０銭）安の６万２２１４円６６銭となった。今週は米大手ハイテク企業の決算発表や日米欧の中央銀行の金融政策決定会合といったイベントを複数控えており、手掛けにくさが意識された。人工知能（ＡＩ）・半導体関連株は軟調な銘柄が目立った一方、それ以外の銘柄では物色意欲もみられ、ＴＯＰＩＸはプラスだった。

・日経平均は小安く始まった後、プラスに切り返す場面もあり方向感欠く。

・アドバンテストなどＡＩ・半導体関連の主力株が売られ指数を下押し。

・東証プライム市場の６割近くが値上がりし、ＴＯＰＩＸは小幅プラス。

・原油価格が高止まりし、鉱業や石油・石炭製品、商社株などしっかり。

・円金利が上昇し、銀行や保険株に物色も。

・ブラジルのルラ大統領の当選確実が伝わり、ブラジル株に連動する上場投資信託（ＥＴＦ）は急落。

・ＴＯＰＩＸは０．３４％高の３９７９．３４ポイントで午前の取引を終了。東証プライム市場の売買代金は３兆２４５４億２０００万円。

・東証３３業種で上昇したのは、鉱業、卸売、石油・石炭の２２業種、下落は非鉄金属、電気機器、機械の１１業種。

・東証プライム市場の騰落数は、値上がりが９００銘柄（５７％）、値下がりは６０５銘柄（３８％）、変わらずは４８銘柄（３％）。

＜ちばぎんアセットマネジメント　調査部長　森田潤氏＞

「今週はイベントが目白押しでもあり、週初から積極的に動きにくく方向感を欠く」

「中銀会合はサプライズ見込まれず、波乱があるとすれば日米ハイテク決算か」

「ＴＯＰＩＸは節目の４０００ポイント割れでＡＩ以外に押し目買いも」

「ＡＩ株は足元で調整進んでおり、決算前に積極的に売る局面でもない」

item.title: World stocks gain ahead of 'formidable' week for risk; oil prices ease
item.description: Global shares advanced on Monday, with investors focused on a week of central bank meetings and corporate earnings that will test confidence in the AI boom.
item.dc:creator: Chris Prentice, Amanda Cooper
item.content:encoded: Global shares advanced on Monday, with investors focused on a week of central bank meetings and corporate earnings that will test confidence in the AI boom. Oil prices retreated after Friday's strong gains, but prices remained near recent highs as persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia kept traders wary. The Houthi group in Yemen said on Monday it had attacked Saudi Arabia's [USN:L2N46C045 TEXT:"East-West crude oil"] pumping stations and Riyadh airport. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) rose 5.05 points, or 0.45%, to 1,124.02. On Wall Street, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were poised for their biggest one-day rallies in more than a month on tech strength after Anthropic's [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"initial public offering"] filing. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 117.37 points, or 0.22%, to 52,332.53, the S&P 500 (.SPX) rose 58.22 points, or 0.76%, to 7,681.90 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) rose 265.87 points, or 1.02%, to 26,220.87. Brazilian stocks posted historic losses. The country's stock exchange [USN:L6N46C031 TEXT:"halted trading"] via a circuit breaker safety mechanism on Monday after [USN:L6N4681ER TEXT:"President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's reelection"]. His opponent refused to concede. In Europe, stocks rebounded on corporate optimism. The STOXX 600 (.STOXX) closed up 0.77%, led by gains in British technology services provider Computacenter (CCC.L) and Danish biotech Genmab (GMAB.CO) . BIG WEEK Traders awaited multiple central bank meetings and earnings from AI hyperscalers. [USN:L6N46919T TEXT:"Earnings"] are in store from Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) , as one-third of S&P 500 companies report. "The combination is formidable: megacap earnings, AI funding concerns, global semiconductor results, five major central bank meetings and potentially market-moving inflation and growth data," said Chris Weston, Pepperstone's head of research. "The danger isn't simply that markets move sharply. It's that one catalyst changes the interpretation of the next, creating feedback loops across equities, rates, FX and volatility," Weston added. [USN:L4N4690C8 TEXT:"New Zealand's"] central bank is widely expected to raise rates on Wednesday. Markets assume the US [USN:L6N46606V TEXT:"Federal Reserve"] will stand pat, but they imply an 80% chance that it will hike rates in December. Much the same is priced in for the [USN:L4N4650KC TEXT:"Bank of Japan"] and the [USN:L6N45U0QU TEXT:"European Central Bank"]. , , A key reading on US core inflation should show cost pressures remained elevated at 3.1% in September, while the economy is forecast to have grown at a brisk 3.2% annualized pace thanks in part to spending on data centers. "The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran," analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a note. "The more extreme and long-lasting the energy shock becomes, the more Fed participants will worry that inflationary pressures could broaden." Emerging market stocks (.MSCIEF) fell 15.27 points, or 0.97%, to 1,562.77. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) closed lower by 0.15%, at 1,505.49. TREASURIES AND CURRENCIES The Brazilian real plunged more than 11% after the presidential election. The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes fell 0.58 basis points to 4.982%. The yield on the benchmark German 10-year Bund rose. In currency markets, the Japanese yen slipped 0.36%, and the euro was down 0.13% after France dodged a [USN:L1N469154 TEXT:"credit downgrade"] last week. The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.25%. Sterling dipped 0.16% , with Britain's new finance minister [USN:L1N46206Z TEXT:"John Healey"] set to deliver his first budget on Wednesday amid rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the US-Israeli war with Iran. Spot gold rose 0.61% to $4,019.96 an ounce, rebounding from the prior session's more than three-month low. US gold futures settled 0.8% higher at $4,038.40 per ounce. Saudi Arabia, which along with Turkey and Pakistan was set to hold talks with Iranian officials in Tehran, said it was important to open channels for negotiations. On Sunday, Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran to try to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the situation said. Brent crude futures fell to $116.01 per barrel, down 0.64% as US crude fell 1.27% to $101.96.

item.title: Lula, Brazil's iconic working class president, wins fourth term in dramatic comeback
item.description: A shock comeback returns Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to power for a fourth term, bucking polls and slowing Latin America’s right-wing surge.
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:
Advertisement

World

Lula, Brazil's iconic working class president, wins fourth term in dramatic comeback

A shock comeback returns Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to power for a fourth term, bucking polls and slowing Latin America’s right-wing surge.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking reelection, waves after voting in the presidential runoff in Sao Bernardo do Campo, Brazil, on Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: AP/Andre Penner)

26 Oct 2026 08:30AM (Updated: 26 Oct 2026 11:40AM)

FAST

SAO PAULO: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term on Sunday (Oct 25), the country's electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The senator, who led the election's first round but lost in the runoff by over 4 million votes, said he would ask for the result to be annulled due to a Sunday Supreme Court ruling that extended voting for two hours. Bolsonaro's refusal to concede defeat has echoes of his father's reaction after losing to Lula in 2022. Former President Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to remain in power.

The scale of Flavio Bolsonaro's loss to Lula - by more than twice his father's losing margin - and the fact his campaign also asked for an extension due to rains in the south, make any annulment unlikely, analysts said. Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE, said there could be right-wing protests in coming days, but "it's very improbable that it will lead to the reversal of the result."

Supporters of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva cheer as presidential runoff results are announced in Sao Paulo, on Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: AP/Natacha Pisarenko)

COMEBACK KING For Lula, his victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election. "He is a statesman, a giant," leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters. At times, Lula's reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers' Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping social changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil's Bovespa index fell nearly 15 per cent in Asia trade on news of Lula's victory. Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula's familiar embrace over Bolsonaro's novelty. "People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights," he said. During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term. He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil's sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power. Lula's win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington's agenda on security and migration. Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist "would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance."

Supporters of Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) gather on a road after polls closed in the presidential runoff election, in Porto Alegre, Brazil, on Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Diego Vara)

LATE-CAMPAIGN BOOST Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round. Previously president from 2003 to 2011, Lula campaigned this year on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians. These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15 per cent increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented. Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil's biggest labour reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress. CHALLENGES AHEAD Still, Lula's fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s. Combined, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable opposition majorities in both chambers. That may deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress on the budget, major legislation and key nominations. Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meagre 2.3 per cent next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82 per cent of GDP, the highest since the pandemic. The president's critics blame spending, though borrowing costs have driven most of the increase in debt. Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model. Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign. The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favour businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could trigger popular backlash.

Meta tells Brazil court it treats Lula and Bolsonaro campaigns equally

Source: Reuters/ec

item.title: Serbia's Vucic concedes defeat in historic election win for student protest movement
item.description: Aleksandar Vucic has held power in Serbia since 2014, and his defeat heralds a new political era for the Balkan country.
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:
Advertisement

World

Serbia's Vucic concedes defeat in historic election win for student protest movement

Aleksandar Vucic has held power in Serbia since 2014, and his defeat heralds a new political era for the Balkan country.

Serbia's former President and the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) prime ministerial candidate Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat during the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia, on Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Zorana Jevtic)

26 Oct 2026 07:40AM (Updated: 26 Oct 2026 09:05AM)

Bookmark

Bookmark

Share

WhatsApp

Click here to return to FAST Tap here to return to FAST

FAST

BELGRADE: Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday (Oct 25) that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country. Vucic, a populist and nationalist, has dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014. But he called snap elections in September after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. "It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won," Vucic said in a televised speech.

Within moments of his announcement, the streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration. Tens of thousands of people thronged along the city's main boulevards, with cars honking, people dancing and students shouting "victory" and "he's done". The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of about 6 million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban in April. It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and a lack of prospects. Vucic said the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament and that his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) would have 105, based on preliminary results. "Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard," said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. "Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future." European leaders and officials congratulated the Student List on its victory, among them President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos. "We stand ready to ... work together to advance Serbia's future in the European Union," von der Leyen wrote on X. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar assured the students of his country's support.

Supporters of the electoral list "Student List - Students Win" celebrate after Aleksandar Vucic, Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) prime ministerial candidate, conceded defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia, on Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Marko Djurica)

RECORD TURNOUT SPURS STUDENTS TO VICTORY Lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put turnout close to 70 per cent, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992. "(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," said voter Katarina Petrovic. Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent and few in the student protest movement dared believe he would concede so fast. Supporters credit him with modernising Serbia's economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals. "Some businessmen, some people will leave us but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition," Vucic said. UNCERTAINTY OVER THE STUDENTS' CANDIDATES Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare. Their list of 250 largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, who was in tears after Vucic's announcement. However, it is unclear who will be prime minister and enact the students' domestic agenda, which aims to root out graft and improve schooling. Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vucic allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the students have been quieter on their international ambitions. As Vucic did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor, Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, and the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner. "The biggest uncertainty is ... who is going to lead the government, who will be the key ministers, and how they will operate based on the promises they made to fight corruption, to reintroduce the rule of law, but also to re-establish Serbia's position in foreign policy," said Radivoje Grujic, a Warsaw-based election consultant. PROTEST MOVEMENT INCREASED PRESSURE The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster started small but quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression worsened in the period since. Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He has said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss. Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a "students are champions" jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number 3, representing the number of the students' list of candidates. "We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words to describe how much," said Andjela, a student who was with a group of friends. Dejan Soskic, a former central bank governor and a candidate of the Student List, called on people to maintain order and peace, and thanked voters for their civilised conduct during the electoral process.

Source: Reuters/dy

item.title: Oil settles lower on peace hopes, Saudi attacks limit losses
item.description: Brent crude futures finished lower on Monday amid hopes of easing hostilities inthe Middle East, but persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia and maritime shipping kept investors wary and prices hovering near six-month highs.
item.dc:creator: Siddharth Cavale
item.content:encoded: Brent crude futures finished lower on Monday amid hopes of easing hostilities in the Middle East , but persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia and maritime shipping kept investors wary and prices hovering near six-month highs. Brent finished the day down 91 cents, or 0.8%, at $115.81 a barrel while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures closed down $1.51, or 1.46%, at $101.76 a barrel. Both benchmarks retreated after strong gains on Friday, when Brent [USN:L1N46903W TEXT:"settled"] more than $3 higher to post a weekly gain of 6%, while WTI rose 2.3% for the week. Investor focus remained on tensions in the Middle East after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they [USN:L2N46C045 TEXT:"struck"] pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pipeline and Riyadh airport over the weekend. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, however, [USN:S8N45V00W TEXT:"said "]on Monday it had destroyed three drones targeting Riyadh and the kingdom's southern regions. Hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in the Middle East conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran and later spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen, weighed on oil prices earlier in the session, with Brent falling more than $2 a barrel. Qatari [USN:S8N43E021 TEXT:"mediators"] travelled to Tehran on Sunday in coordination with the United States to seek ways to ease regional tensions, according to an official briefed on the matter. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan[USN:L2N46C041 TEXT:"held talks"] with Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday as part of efforts to prevent further escalation in the region. The talks were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations, which signed a mutual defence pact in August. At the conclusion, the four countries agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation in peace and security, Iranian state media reported. Egypt's parliament authorized President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself, raising the prospect of Egyptian military support for the kingdom. WORST MONTH FOR MARITIME ATTACKS The effects of the US-Israeli war with Iran that began on February 28 continue to reverberate as companies adjust to the disruptions of [USN:L1N4690RP TEXT:"commercial shipping"] through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait caused by the conflict. [USN:L1N4690RP TEXT:"October"] has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. An [USN:L4N469189 TEXT:"oil spill"] from a strike-damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency [USN:S8N45V000 TEXT:"said "]on Monday it had received third-party reports of a vessel on fire near Al-Faw, Iraq, adding that the crew's status, extent of any damage and any environmental impact were unknown. Elsewhere, [USN:L6N46C0P1 TEXT:"Russian refiners"] are raising diesel production in October after the government granted export quotas following the Kremlin's supply agreement with the United States, two industry people close to the matter said. Energy ministers from Saudi Arabia and Singapore said state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco would start [USN:L2N46C022 TEXT:"storing"] crude oil in Singapore from the second half of 2027, to make Aramco's supply chain in the region more resilient. The [USN:P8N3RS06K TEXT:"head"] of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, reiterated supply concerns, saying on Monday at an industry event in Singapore that he did not expect energy markets in 2027 to return to where they were before the Iran war. In the US, stocks of crude oil in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 282.6 million barrels last week, the lowest level since October 1982, the Department of Energy said on Monday.

Supporters of Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for re-election, gather outside a polling station after the arrival of Brazil's presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) to cast his vote during the presidential runoff election, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Oct 25, 2026. BRASILIA: Brazil's Supreme Court extended voting in the country's presidential election by two hours on Sunday (Oct 25), leading the electoral authority to pause a vote count that had already started publishing early-stage results. The election pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Polls were initially set to close at 5pm Brasilia time (4am Monday, Singapore time) and will now close at 7pm after Supreme Justice Cristiano Zanin accepted a request by Lula's campaign to extend voting, pointing to public transportation issues in three cities in the state of Bahia. Zanin's decision landed right around the 5pm cutoff, when the electoral court had already started publishing results that showed Lula leading Bolsonaro with 0.25 per cent of ballot counted. Lula had 57.66 per cent of votes, compared with 42.34 per cent for Bolsonaro, the early count showed.

After the Zanin ruling, the TSE said it would pause the vote count to allow for the extended voting window to close.

Related:

Lula and Bolsonaro spar in Brazil poll debate

PAUSE ADDS UNCERTAINTY The pause over the vote count injects uncertainty into a Brazilian electoral process still grappling with the fallout from 2022, when Jair Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat to Lula. His supporters later invaded government buildings in protests against the result, and Bolsonaro received a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup. Lula had asked electoral authorities to extend voting in at least nine states after his campaign alleged some officials reduced election day public transportation, impacting voters' ability to get to the polls. Earlier on Sunday, a court in Bahia, a Lula stronghold in the Northeast, ordered the arrest of a top transportation official in the city of Salvador over allegations that he directed a reduction in the city’s bus fleet. Bolsonaro had also asked for voting to be extended in at least three states, citing bad weather.

KYIV: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said US warnings about imminent Russian ballistic missile strikes , critical to Ukraine's air defences, had been fully restored after recent issues. Speaking to Ukraine's TSN television channel, he said SpaceX's Starshield satellite internet had been working at speeds of up to 420kmh since early on Saturday (Oct 24) morning, after it had been throttled earlier in October amid diplomatic pressure on Kyiv from Washington. Zelenskyy said he discussed both issues in a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, casting the changes as results of that meeting. Speaking about the upcoming technical talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in November, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would not discuss limits to its armed forces, or enforced post-war neutrality. Kyiv has long sought entry into the NATO alliance despite the reticence of some members. Zelenskyy also renewed his push for a trilateral US-brokered meeting between him and Vladimir Putin. The Ukrainian leader has long argued Putin is the only person in Russia who can make major decisions to end the war or meaningfully discuss core issues, such as the fate of the nearly 20 per cent of Ukraine that Russia occupies. "The issue of territories is a red line that can be discussed exclusively at the level of leaders," Zelenskyy said.

JERUSALEM: Billionaire American investor Bill Ackman on Sunday (Oct 25) said that Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich should not serve in Israel's next government, saying the two far-right politicians had caused enormous damage to the country's reputation. The public intervention by the prominent hedge fund manager, who is Jewish, comes just two days before Israel's general election, in which polls show a tight race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition and the opposition. Ackman wrote on X that from the perspective of someone who had an understanding of how Israel was perceived in the United States, "Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions." BOTH MINISTERS HAVE FACED SANCTIONS The founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, who praised Netanyahu last week, said a government without the two ministers would send a message that Israel was "turning a new page."

"This will allow Israel to rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans at large," he said. The Abraham Accords are the 2020 agreement, mediated by President Donald Trump's first administration, that saw Israel establish relations with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. It later reestablished official ties with Morocco. Representatives for Ben-Gvir and Smotrich did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Related:

Thousands rally in Tel Aviv against Netanyahu ahead of vote

Middle East conflict: Israel faces pressure from Western allies over Gaza and West Bank

As ministers in Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have overseen policies widely perceived as discriminatory against Israel's minority Arab population and Palestinians living in the occupied West Bank. Several countries, including Britain, Canada and Australia, have imposed sanctions on the two ministers over accusations that they have incited violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party is projected to win around 10 parliamentary seats at Tuesday's election, up from 6, while Smotrich's Religious Zionism is projected to win 8, up from 7. Ackman, who was visiting Israel last week, and who along with his wife Neri Oxman owns 5 percent of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, supported Donald Trump's candidacy for president in 2024. Trump last week publicly endorsed Netanyahu for prime minister. Nimrod Goren, the president of Israeli think tank Mitvim, said Ackman's statement appeared to reflect a desire among Trump's circles for Netanyahu to drop his far-right allies after the vote to form a 'unity government' with opposition parties. However, Gadi Eisenkot, the leading challenger to Netanyahu, and other opposition party leaders have ruled out forming a government with Israel's longest-serving prime minister. Speaking at a Tel Aviv conference on Thursday, Ackman praised Netanyahu, who he said had done a good job in protecting and defending Israel since the Oct 7 2023 Hamas attack. Thousands of Israelis rallied in Tel Aviv on Saturday calling for an independent inquiry into the attack that killed around 1,200 people.

Source: Reuters/fs

LONDON: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants a discussion about returning to the European Union's freedom of movement rules for workers, a key issue in the 2016 Brexit referendum which led to Britain leaving the bloc. Building on previous comments about the need to rethink ties with Brussels, Burnham told the Sunday Times that the influx of EU workers into Britain before Brexit had posed very significant challenges. "But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn't as difficult (as now)," he said. "Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things." Official data has shown long-term net migration in 2025 fell to close to its level before a new post-Brexit immigration system was introduced at the start of 2021.

In September, two months after replacing Keir Starmer as Labour Party leader and prime minister, Burnham said Britain should consider options for its relationship with the EU, including possibly rejoining the bloc one day. He had previously backed the pledges of Starmer's government which included no return to freedom of movement which Brussels sets as a condition for being part of the bloc's single market. In his interview with the Sunday Times, conducted on Oct 19, Burnham said the issue of freedom of movement could be considered as part of a broader reset of Britain's relationship with the EU, including on data sharing and migration.

Related:

Burnham hopes for EU deal next month, stirs Brexit debate

'Welcome back,' says Macron, as UK PM opens door to EU return

"You've got to see it in the round, rather than just looking at freedom of movement on its own," he said. Burnham, who is trying to find ways to speed up Britain's economy, is due to meet top EU officials for a summit on Nov 20. He said he could not imagine recommending that Britain adopt the euro currency or the EU's border-free travel arrangements. A new referendum would be needed to rejoin the EU but not necessarily to join the bloc's single market or a customs union, the Sunday Times quoted Burnham as saying. Former Conservative finance minister Jeremy Hunt, who campaigned to stay in the EU in 2016, said it would be a mistake to reopen one of the fundamental debates of the referendum and he said relaxing immigration rules would hurt people in Britain. "I think it will be a hammer blow to getting people off welfare and into work," Hunt told Sky News.

Source: Reuters/fs

item.title: Macron says Paris suburb shooting that killed one person was terrorist and racist act
item.description: A gunman killed one person and wounded five others, including a 12-year-old girl, in a shooting in a Paris suburb that French President Emmanuel Macron described as a "terrorist and racist" attack..
item.dc:creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: A gunman killed one person and wounded five others, including a 12-year-old girl, in a shooting in a Paris suburb that French President Emmanuel Macron described as a "terrorist and racist" attack.. "What happened today is, I am telling you, a turning point, because it is the first time we have had a terrorist act that was planned to kill our compatriots, our children, based on the colour of their skin or their religion," Macron told reporters. The shooting happened earlier on Friday when the gunman fired an automatic weapon at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children's playground in Trappes, on the Paris outskirts. Officials said a 39-year-old suspect, whom they named as Kevin T, had been arrested. His family surname was not given, as is common practice in such criminal inquiries in France. Kevin T denied the attack was racist, Olivier Christen, France's national anti-terrorism prosecutor, told reporters on Monday. The shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France, after nationwide protests [USN:L1N46908B TEXT:"turned violent"] last Saturday and before further demonstrations this coming weekend. Some far-right politicians have blamed immigration for looting and vandalism in a number of French cities on October 17. Macron said the gunman had deliberately chosen not to fire upon some people due to their skin colour and appearance. The anti-terrorism prosecutor's office, known as PNAT, formally opened an investigation into the shooting. PNAT can [USN:L8N3SB03W TEXT:"take over any criminal investigation"] it believes meets the criteria for terrorism, including violence inspired by far-right ideas. Terrorism sentences are tougher, and counter-terrorism forces have greater investigative powers. Broadcaster BFM said the wounded girl had been hit eight times and was in serious condition. Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh, whose parents came from Morocco, said the shooting was "racist" and "Islamophobic." "The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law," said Rabeh. Rabeh called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that "ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts." Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of nearby La Verriere, said the suspect was "of a European type." Rabeh said two of the victims were of African and North African origin, respectively, and did not provide details about the backgrounds of the other victims. Video images showed the suspect's car riddled with bullets.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Anthropic [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"took the wraps off its US initial public offering filing"] on Monday, bringing the Claude maker a step closer to a landmark debut that is set to test investor appetite for the rapidly growing AI industry. The listing would represent what is expected to be one of the largest debuts ever attempted, potentially reshaping benchmark indexes, investor flows and the broader narrative driving US equities. "A successful IPO from Anthropic could crack open or slam shut the IPO market, even well into 2027," said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, a provider of IPO-focused research and ETFs. A GLANCE AT WORLD'S BIGGEST IPOs The biggest IPOs globally, ranked by deal size: Here is an overview of some of the mega IPOs: ANTHROPIC By unveiling its hotly anticipated US IPO filing, AI lab Anthropic took a crucial step towards a potential roadshow launch. The filing confirmed a series of Reuters exclusives that offered an early peek at its contents before Anthropic made it public, including details of its financial performance, growth trajectory and IPO plans. Some current and prospective investors are valuing Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion that investors had previously expected after the AI startup disclosed some financial details at a [USN:L6N4601DE TEXT:"recent investor event"]. The IPO has already been pushed back from earlier plans, with Reuters previously reporting that marketing was expected to begin in mid-October at the earliest. The AI heavyweight is [USN:L6N45317D TEXT:"seeking to raise"] as much as $100 billion in the IPO, Reuters has reported. Anthropic, which had revealed in June that it [USN:L4N4291DK TEXT:"confidentially filed"] for a US IPO, [USN:L4N4251V1 TEXT:"raised $65 billion"] at a post-money valuation of $965 billion in late May. OPENAI OpenAI, which operates AI chatbot ChatGPT, revealed in June that it had [USN:L4N41X1KD TEXT:"confidentially filed"] for a US IPO. The company [USN:L6N45500D TEXT:"will not go public in 2026"], CEO Sam Altman had said in September, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence that render "unacceptable" even a 10% risk that AI could cause human extinction by decade's end. OpenAI is [USN:L1N4610T9 TEXT:"racing to secure investor commitments"] before rival Anthropic's expected public market debut in mid-November, in an unusually fast fundraising that could value the ChatGPT maker at over $1.4 trillion, Reuters has reported. In May, OpenAI fended off an [USN:L1N41V0VT TEXT:"existential court challenge from Elon Musk"], simplifying the path for it to proceed with a stock market listing. "We have not decided on timing yet; it may be a while because there are things we want to do that are likely easier as a private company. But it's a complicated set of tradeoffs and this gives us the option to go public sooner if that ends up being best," OpenAI had said in June. SPACEX Elon Musk's rocket and satellite maker SpaceX made its [USN:L1N42K06V TEXT:"historic stock market debut"] on the Nasdaq in June, shattering records and eclipsing Saudi Aramco's 2019 listing by a wide margin to become the largest IPO ever. The IPO [USN:L4N42C0IF TEXT:"upended traditions"] with its record $75 billion listing, breaking away from the normal IPO process by setting the price before meetings with investors at a roadshow, which Wall Street always uses to test demand and set a price range. At $75 billion, the IPO's proceeds were more than double those of Saudi Aramco's record-setting 2019 IPO. SpaceX shares ended their first day of trading at $160.95 per share to bring its value to $2.1 trillion. The stock has since lost some of its momentum and closed at $147.49 on October 23, 9.3% above the $135 IPO price.

item.title: OFRMO Summary
item.description: "Retour vers le futur" au Brésil? Flavio Bolsonaro, comme jadis son père, refuse de reconnaître la victoire de Lula
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: "Retour vers le futur" au Brésil? Flavio Bolsonaro, comme jadis son père, refuse de reconnaître la victoire de Lula SÃO PAULO, 26 octobre (Reuters) - Le candidat de la droite brésilienne Flavio Bolsonaro emboîte le pas à son père, l'ex-président condamné pour tentative de coup d'Etat après la présidentielle perdue de 2022, en refusant de reconnaître sa défaite face au président sortant Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, qui a remporté dimanche un quatrième mandat historique. Le pape se rendra comme prévu en Amérique latine en novembre CITE DU VATICAN, 26 octobre (Reuters) - Le pape Léon XIV, opéré le 13 octobre dernier d'une tumeur cancéreuse au poumon droit, se rendra comme prévu en Uruguay, en Argentine et au Pérou du 6 au 17 novembre prochains, ses médecins estimant qu'il est suffisamment remis pour effectuer ce voyage, annonce lundi le Vatican. Russie: Arrestation de deux suspects après une tentative d'attaque pour le compte de l'Ukraine annonce le FSB MOSCOU, 26 octobre (Reuters) - Le renseignement russe (FSB) a annoncé lundi l'arrestation de deux hommes soupçonnés d'une tentative d'attaque de drones pour le compte de l'Ukraine contre la défense anti-aérienne russe à Moscou et une installation électrique de la capitale. Jordanie: Arrestation de trois suspects après une attaque meurtrière contre une église AL-JUDAYYDA, Jordanie, LE CAIRE, 26 octobre (Reuters) - Les forces de sécurité jordaniennes ont arrêté trois suspects après l'attaque meurtrière perpétrée vendredi contre une église dans le sud du pays, rapporte lundi la télévision d'État. Bulgarie: Second tour entre la présidente sortante Iotova et Gyurov le 1er novembre SOFIA, 26 octobre (Reuters) - La présidente sortante Iliana Iotova, arrivée dimanche en tête du premier tour de l'élection présidentielle en Bulgarie avec plus de 34% des voix, affrontera le 1er novembre l'ex-Premier ministre par intérim Andrey Gyurov lors d'un second tour qui s'annonce serré, entre tenants du dialogue avec Moscou et partisans d'un rapprochement avec les Occidentaux. Ukraine: Des frappes russes visent plusieurs régions, des blessés 26 octobre (Reuters) - Des frappes russes menées dans la nuit de dimanche à lundi ont fait six blessés dans le sud-est et le nord de l'Ukraine, ont dit un responsable et les services d'urgence ukrainiens. Chine: Le 5e plénum du PCC mise sur des mesures de gouvernance fermes PÉKIN, 26 octobre (Reuters) - Le cinquième plénum du comité central du Parti communiste chinois (PCC) s'est ouvert ce lundi pour quatre jours durant lesquels les dirigeants du pays discuteront de mesures visant à instaurer une "autogestion complète et rigoureuse du Parti" alors que Xi Jinping cherche à renforcer son autorité et à imposer une uniformité idéologique. Lula crée la surprise et remporte l'élection présidentielle au Brésil BRASILIA/SÃO PAULO, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Le président sortant Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a remporté dimanche un nouveau mandat à la tête du Brésil, a annoncé le tribunal électoral national, un résultat surprenant alors que les sondages donnaient son adversaire, le sénateur de droite Flavio Bolsonaro, en tête. La prix Nobel Maria Corina Machado est rentrée au Venezuela La cheffe de file de l'opposition vénézuélienne, Maria Corina Machado, a annoncé dimanche être rentrée dans son pays après avoir passé près d'un an dans la clandestinité à l'étranger. Aleksandar Vucic concède la défaite aux élections législatives en Serbie Le dirigeant populiste Aleksandar Vucic a concédé la défaite aux élections législatives, alors que les Serbes se sont massivement rendus aux urnes dimanche pour chasser du pouvoir un président que nombre d'entre eux, à commencer par les étudiants qui ont multiplié les manifestations depuis deux ans, accusent de corruption.
